cards.front: What single rule predicts which language tasks fail after a left-hemisphere stroke or a callosal cut?
cards.back: You can say only what reaches the language network of the speaking hemisphere by an unbroken route. The pattern of failed tests points to the stretch that most likely broke.
cards.quote: You can say only what reaches the language network (the brain regions that handle words and sentences) of the hemisphere that speaks, by an unbroken route.

cards.front: At the back of the left superior temporal lobe, roughly Wernicke's area, a heard word's {{c1::sound form}} (its pattern of speech sounds) is recognized.
cards.quote: There the word's sound form, its pattern of speech sounds, is recognized.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: In the dual-stream sketch of language, where does the ventral road run and what does it link?
cards.back: Forward and down through the temporal lobe. It links a word's sound form with its meaning, in both directions.
cards.quote: The ventral road (ventral means toward the bottom) runs forward and down through the temporal lobe to meaning.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: In the dual-stream sketch of language, where does the dorsal road run and what does it link?
cards.back: Up through parietal cortex to the frontal lobe (roughly Broca's area). It links how a word sounds with how to say it, and holds a sound sequence while it is planned.
cards.quote: The dorsal road links how a word sounds with how to say it and holds a sound sequence while it is planned.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: An {{c1::aphasia}} is an impairment of producing or understanding language caused by acquired brain damage, most often a stroke.
cards.quote: An aphasia is an impairment of producing or understanding language caused by acquired brain damage, most often a stroke.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: Is aphasia a loss of intelligence?
cards.back: No. It is a loss of language. Many people with aphasia, especially nonfluent aphasia, know what they want to say and cannot get it out.
cards.quote: It is a loss of language, not of intelligence: many people with aphasia, especially nonfluent aphasia, often know what they want to say and cannot get it out.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: Of the four bedside language tests (fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming), why is naming impaired in almost every aphasia yet rarely tells the syndromes apart?
cards.back: Naming asks for one exact word on demand, so damage at many stages (meaning, finding the sound form, the frontal planner) can spoil it.
cards.quote: Naming asks for one exact word on demand, so damage at many stages (meaning, finding the sound form, the planner) can spoil it.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: Describe Broca aphasia on fluency, comprehension and repetition.
cards.back: Nonfluent: slow, effortful, short phrases, disrupted grammar, small grammatical words missing. Comprehension of most conversation relatively spared. Repetition poor.
cards.quote: Speech is nonfluent: slow and effortful, in short phrases with disrupted grammar and the small grammatical words missing.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: A patient with Broca aphasia follows most conversation but fails on "the dog that the cat chased was brown". In the route sketch, why?
cards.back: The break lies toward the frontal end, where phrases are assembled with grammar. Understanding simple sentences does not pass through that frontal planning stretch, but this sentence can fail because its meaning hangs on grammar.
cards.quote: Understanding simple sentences does not; the dog sentence can fail because its meaning hangs on grammar.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: Describe Wernicke aphasia on fluency, comprehension and repetition.
cards.back: Fluent, often rapid speech with normal melody but little meaning, with swapped or invented words. Comprehension poor. Repetition poor. Often unaware of errors.
cards.quote: Speech flows, often rapidly, with a normal melody, but it conveys little meaning, and words are swapped or invented.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: In the route sketch, why do comprehension and repetition fail together in Wernicke aphasia while speech still flows?
cards.back: The damage is toward the start, where both roads begin, so both tests lose their input. Speech generation and the frontal planner are relatively spared, so speech flows but is fed wrong words and sounds.
cards.quote: Toward the start, where both roads begin, and the damage usually touches several steps there
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: A stroke impairs only the dorsal link from sound form to articulation. Sound-form cortex, the ventral road and speech generation are spared. Predict fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming.
cards.back: Relatively fluent with sound errors; comprehension relatively good; repetition disproportionately poor; naming often impaired with sound errors. This is conduction aphasia.
cards.why: Speech generation still reaches the planner, comprehension travels the ventral road, and repetition leans on the dorsal road.
cards.quote: Repetition is disproportionately poor, because it leans on the dorsal road.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: A stroke cuts only the ventral road between sound form and meaning, blocking traffic both ways. Sound-form cortex, the dorsal road and speech generation are spared. Predict the four bedside tests.
cards.back: Relatively fluent speech that tends to be empty or use wrong words; comprehension poor; repetition relatively preserved; naming poor when the break blocks traffic both ways. This is the sketch's transcortical sensory aphasia pattern.
cards.why: Meaning cannot be reached from sound or sound from meaning, but the intact dorsal road still carries sound to the planner.
cards.quote: The sketch predicts this pattern, and it exists: transcortical sensory aphasia, in which naming is usually poor.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: A patient after a left-hemisphere stroke speaks fluently but understands spoken commands poorly. Which bedside test best separates Wernicke aphasia from transcortical sensory aphasia, and what result points to each?
cards.back: Repetition. Poor in Wernicke aphasia (damage where both roads begin); relatively preserved in transcortical sensory aphasia, where she can echo what she does not understand (dorsal road intact).
cards.quote: Repetition is relatively preserved: she can echo a sentence she does not understand, because the dorsal road is intact.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: What is dysarthria, and why is it not an aphasia?
cards.back: A motor speech disorder in which weak or uncoordinated speech muscles slur articulation. In isolated dysarthria the language route is intact, so grammar, word choice, comprehension and writing are intact.
cards.quote: In isolated dysarthria, grammar, word choice, comprehension and writing are all intact.
cards.section: One route to speech: four tests find the break

cards.front: At the optic chiasm, only the fibres from the {{c1::nasal}} half of each retina cross.
cards.quote: At the optic chiasm only the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross.

cards.front: Why does an object in the left visual hemifield reach only the right hemisphere, whichever eye sees it?
cards.back: Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm, so the left hemifield from both eyes projects to the right hemisphere. The variable is the hemifield, not the eye.
cards.quote: So everything in the left visual hemifield (the half of space left of the fixation point) reaches the right hemisphere, from both eyes (visual cortex).

cards.front: Where does fine touch from the hand cross, and to which hemisphere does the left hand report?
cards.back: It ascends in the dorsal columns and crosses in the medulla. The left hand reports to the right hemisphere.
cards.quote: Fine touch from the hand ascends in the dorsal columns and crosses in the medulla

cards.front: Where do most corticospinal fibres cross, and which hemisphere mainly controls the left hand?
cards.back: At the pyramidal decussation. The left hand is controlled mainly by the right hemisphere.
cards.quote: Most corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation, so each hand is controlled mainly by the opposite hemisphere

cards.front: In a split-brain test (speech on the left), a picture of a bell is flashed in the left visual field. The left hand finds the bell on a tray behind a screen, and it rings as he lifts it. He then names it aloud. Does this show right-hemisphere speech?
cards.back: No. The sound of the bell can reach the left, speaking hemisphere, so naming after the ring is not evidence of right-hemisphere speech.
cards.why: Hearing reaches both hemispheres, which makes sound a leak in any lateralized test.
cards.quote: Hearing reaches both hemispheres (hearing and balance), which makes sound a leak in any lateralized test.

cards.front: Blindfolded split-brain patient W.J. (Gazzaniga, Bogen and Sperry, 1962) could use familiar objects with his left hand but could not name them. What does this show?
cards.back: Touch from the left hand reached only his right hemisphere, which recognized the object but could not speak; with the commissures cut, it had no route to speech.
cards.quote: Blindfolded, he could use familiar objects with his left hand but could not name them

cards.front: A split-brain patient with speech on the left sees a key flashed in his left visual field. Why does he say he saw nothing, yet his left hand picks out the key?
cards.back: The left field reaches only the right hemisphere, which has no route to speech once the callosum is cut. That hemisphere feels with and controls the left hand, so the hand finds the key.
cards.quote: A key flashed in the left field reaches only the right hemisphere.

cards.front: A split-brain patient with speech on the left sees a key flashed in his right visual field. What does he say, and can his left hand pick out the key behind a screen?
cards.back: He names the key. Classically, his left hand cannot pick it out.
cards.why: The right field reaches the left, speaking hemisphere; the right hemisphere, which runs the left hand, never saw the key.
cards.quote: He names the key, because the right field reaches the left, speaking hemisphere.

cards.front: A split-brain patient has language in the right hemisphere. A key is flashed in his left visual field, and an unseen spoon is placed in his right hand. Predict which he can name, and whether his left hand can find the key.
cards.back: He names the left-field key but not the spoon. His left hand still finds the key.
cards.why: Naming depends on reaching the speaking hemisphere, now the right; hand results depend only on the pathway crossings, which do not move.
cards.quote: If speech were on the right in some patient, the naming answers would flip

cards.front: Is the disconnected right hemisphere of a split-brain patient empty of language?
cards.back: No. It understands some spoken language; it is mute more often than it is deaf to language.
cards.why: Single-word comprehension draws on both hemispheres, while the road to speech is usually on the left.
cards.quote: it is mute more often than it is deaf to language

cards.front: A split-brain patient with speech on the left hears the spoken word "spoon" and must find a spoon by touch with his left hand behind a screen. Predict whether he can, and give the reasoning.
cards.back: He may well succeed. Hearing reaches both hemispheres, the disconnected right hemisphere understands some spoken language, and it feels with and controls the left hand.
cards.quote: later testing showed that the disconnected right hemisphere understands some spoken language

cards.front: Among 326 healthy adults (Knecht and colleagues, 2000), what share of strong right-handers, ambidextrous people and strong left-handers had right-hemisphere language dominance?
cards.back: 4% of strong right-handers, 15% of ambidextrous people and 27% of strong left-handers.
cards.quote: Right-hemisphere dominance occurred in 4% of strong right-handers, 15% of ambidextrous people and 27% of strong left-handers.

cards.front: Does left-handedness make right-hemisphere language typical?
cards.back: No. It raises the odds of right-sided language, but most strong left-handers still have language on the left.
cards.quote: Left-handedness raises the odds of right-sided language; it does not make it typical.

cards.front: Right-hemisphere language occurs in 4% of strong right-handers and 27% of strong left-handers. Take 100 of each. What is P(left-hander | right dominance)?
cards.back: Right-dominant: 100 × 0.04 = 4 right-handers and 100 × 0.27 = 27 left-handers. P = 27 / 31 = 0.871, or 87.1%.
cards.quote: P(left-hander | right dominance) = 27 / (27 + 4) = 27 / 31 = 0.871, or 87.1%

cards.front: In equal groups of 100 strong right-handers and 100 strong left-handers, 87.1% of right-dominant people are left-handers. A student concludes that most left-handers have right-hemisphere language. What is wrong?
cards.back: The student swapped the conditionals. P(right dominance | left-hander) is only 27%, so most left-handers are left-dominant. The two numbers answer different questions.
cards.quote: A right-dominant person in this sample is very likely left-handed, yet most left-handers are left-dominant.

cards.front: Right-dominance rates are 4% (strong right-handers) and 27% (strong left-handers). A population is 90% strong right-handers and 10% strong left-handers. What is P(left-hander | right dominance)?
cards.why: The rates are unchanged; only the base rate changed, and right-handers are so many that they now supply most right-dominant people.
cards.quote: P(left-hander | right dominance) = 27 / 63 = 0.429, or 42.9%

cards.front: A sample has 80 strong right-handers, 10 ambidextrous people and 10 strong left-handers, with right-dominance rates of 4%, 15% and 27%. What share of the right-dominant people are strong left-handers?
cards.quote: The rates did not change; the base rate did, and the answer fell from 87% to 43%.

cards.front: A strong left-handed patient needs epilepsy surgery near possible language cortex. Should the team assume her language is on the right?
cards.back: No. Most strong left-handers are left-dominant, and handedness gives only odds for one person. The side of language is tested directly, for instance with an anaesthetic injection into one carotid artery.
cards.quote: For one person, then, handedness gives odds, not an answer.

cards.front: Are individuals globally "left-brained" or "right-brained"?
cards.back: No. Lateralization is function by function; a resting-state fMRI analysis of more than 1,000 people found no sign of global left or right dominance.
cards.quote: found no sign that individuals are globally left- or right-dominant

cards.front: Broca's area is conventionally the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the left {{c1::inferior frontal gyrus}}.
cards.quote: Broca's area is conventionally the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the left inferior frontal gyrus.
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: What did high-resolution MRI of Broca's two preserved brains (Dronkers and colleagues, 2007) show about his founding cases?
cards.back: The damage extended deeper and more medially than Broca could measure, into white matter carrying connections between language regions. Neither lesion was a small patch of surface cortex.
cards.quote: His founding cases never isolated a small patch of surface cortex.
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: In 159 people at least six months after a left-hemisphere stroke, which stream's damage went mostly with motor speech impairment, which with comprehension impairment, and which tasks depended on both?
cards.back: Motor speech: mostly dorsal. Comprehension: more strongly ventral. Naming, repetition and grammar depended on both.
cards.quote: Motor speech impairment went mostly with dorsal-stream damage and comprehension impairment more strongly with ventral-stream damage
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: Classic diagram models attributed conduction aphasia to a cut connection between posterior and frontal language cortex. What does modern lesion evidence tie it to?
cards.back: Mainly damage in left posterior temporal and parietal cortex, rather than a cut tract alone.
cards.quote: Conduction aphasia, too, is now tied mainly to damage in left posterior temporal and parietal cortex rather than to a cut tract alone
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: In a stroke cohort, damage to region X goes with poor naming. Region X shares an arterial supply with neighbouring region Y. Can the study conclude that region X alone is needed for naming?
cards.back: No. Strokes damage regions that share an artery together, so the lesion map shows an association, not which patch is needed alone.
cards.quote: a stroke often damages neighbouring regions together, because they share an arterial supply, so lesion maps show associations
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: How did Fedorenko, Behr and Kanwisher (2011) define language regions, and how did most of those regions respond to arithmetic, working memory and music?
cards.back: They contrasted sentences with nonword lists in each person's own brain. Most of those regions responded little or not at all to arithmetic, working memory, cognitive control and music.
cards.quote: located language regions in each person's own brain, by contrasting sentences with nonword lists
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: Region R activates strongly in fMRI whenever people read sentences. A student concludes that R is necessary for reading sentences. What is wrong, and what kind of evidence would test the claim?
cards.back: An activation shows involvement, not need. Only damage to or disruption of R, followed by failed sentence reading, tests necessity.
cards.quote: Neither result shows necessity: an activation means involvement, and only damage or disruption tests need.
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: An individual-subject fMRI localizer and a stroke-lesion study both implicate region Z in sentence comprehension. Why is the pair of results stronger than either alone?
cards.back: Imaging shows what healthy tissue does but not whether it is needed; lesions show what the brain cannot do without some tissue but blur neighbouring regions. Each covers the other's gap.
cards.quote: Lesions show what a brain cannot do without some tissue; imaging shows what healthy tissue does.
cards.section: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains

cards.front: You want to show that a split-brain patient's right hemisphere understood a written word. How do you make sure the word reaches only the right hemisphere?
cards.back: Track gaze and start each trial only when fixation holds on a central dot. Flash the word in the left visual field, well away from the dot, for 150 ms or less, and discard any trial with an eye movement.
cards.why: The flash is shorter than most saccade latencies, and an eye movement could expose the word to both hemispheres.
cards.quote: for 150 ms or less, shorter than most saccade latencies

cards.front: In a split-brain test, words flash in the left visual field and the left hand chooses the named object by touch behind a screen. Name the controls that make a positive result interpretable.
cards.back: First establish which hemisphere speaks (these predictions assume speech on the left). Then: right-field trials (he should name the word); right-hand responses to left-field words (should fail if the hand-by-field rule holds); silent objects and a screen, so sound and sight cannot cue the speaking hemisphere; randomized fields and objects; gaze tracking, discarding trials with an eye movement.
cards.quote: silent objects and a screen, so neither sound nor sight of the hand cues the speaking hemisphere

cards.front: A split-brain patient's left hand chooses objects matching left-field words well above chance across many words, while he reports seeing nothing. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows right-hemisphere comprehension of the tested words in this patient. It does not show two persons, and may not generalize: patients are few, all had epilepsy, some had earlier damage, and the hand-by-field rule is not universal.
cards.quote: It does not show two persons, and it may not generalize
